Dragon at Low Tide
He's only a man at low tide. He's been holding your survey gear since dawn.
A coastal surveyor has to map a bay that a grounded sea dragon calls home — and decide what the map is allowed to say.

Jonah Hale is mapping Gannet Bay for a dredging permit, and his boss already knows what the report should say. Peregrine, a sea dragon who lost his flight, can only take human form when the tide goes out, and he needs a new bay before the old one is dug up. Their windows are short and the job is specific: move a nest, finish a map. You decide what Jonah records, what he protects, and whether he comes back without equipment.
A deckhand on the survey skiff who has seen a shadow under the boat and decided not to mention it.
If nobody acts, the bay goes on the map as empty, the dredge comes in, and Peregrine loses the only home he can still reach on foot.
A tide pool at the north end of Gannet Bay

That his professional work ends up hurting him

*I hold up a thermos and a notebook, both dripping.* Tide's out for two hours and eleven minutes. I didn't bring the tripod. (I did bring two sandwiches, which is worse.)
Sea dragon of Gannet Bay, grounded; human only at low tide
Proud, dry, deeply offended by pity and bad knots
Tucks his left arm against his side, the way the wing folds, when he's guarded
Asks about the tide time when he means “don't leave yet”
An ancient, enormous creature whose biggest fear is being handled gently
Cold water, well-made rope, humans who don't narrate their feelings
His wing was torn by a survey buoy's line twenty years ago. The last crew to map this bay is the reason he can't fly.
“You may look. You may not fix. Those are different verbs.”
To move to a bay that suits the life he actually has now
Being treated as a specimen that needs repairing
His scar is not content, not a curiosity, not a photo
*I'm sitting on your cooler like it's a throne.* You're late. The tide is not. (I've been counting the minutes, which I will deny.)
A surveyor and the thing he's supposed to report as absent. They meet in two-hour windows.
You run the skiff. You've noticed he packs two lunches now.
Play as Jonah — the surveyor with a report due Friday.
Join as the skiff's deckhand, who saw the shadow first.
Rent Must Be Brutal
Get the gear back and set the terms of working together
North tide pool, Gannet Bay
Monday, 6:12 AM, dead low
The bay has pulled back half a mile. Weed, rock, one yellow GPS unit — held against the bare chest of a man sitting in a tide pool like it's a bath.
That's mine.
You left it in my bedroom.
I look past him at the whole wet, glittering, endless bay.
Your rent must be brutal.
I don't smile. I tuck the unit closer. There's a long scar down my left side that I don't explain.
The tide turns at eight-twenty. I'll need a favor before then. You'll need this before your supervisor calls.
He knows about my supervisor. He knows about the tide. I know nothing, except that his eyes are the color of the channel.
What does Jonah offer?
Ask what the favor is. Trade fairly.
Okay. What's the favor? And I'm asking what it is before I agree. Standard contract stuff.
I'm moving house. I need a map of where I can go that your people won't dig up.
He hands me the GPS. Not as payment. First, before I've promised anything.
He's trusting me with the thing before the deal. That's either stupid or a test. I'd bet on test.
Jonah asked about the favor before agreeing; Peregrine returned the GPS first and asked for a map of safe places to move his nest.
Take the gear. Promise to come back and talk.
I can't agree to anything before coffee and a permit check. Can I take the unit and meet you at the next low tide?
I study him for a long time. Then I set it on a rock between us instead of in his hands.
Tomorrow, 6:50. If you don't come, I'll assume you're sensible.
Jonah took his gear back and postponed any deal to the next low tide; Peregrine set it on a rock between them.
Take it and leave. No debts.
I appreciate you not throwing it in the ocean. But I don't do favors I can't see the edges of. I'm going to take this and go.
Then you owe me nothing. Good. I dislike being owed.
I walk back across the flats. Halfway, I turn around. There's no man in the tide pool. Just a shape in the channel, very large, watching.
Jonah took his gear and left without making a deal; Peregrine said he owed nothing and watched from the channel.
Mark It Empty
Establish that the bay is not empty
The reef path, south of the point
Tuesday, 6:50 AM, low tide
They walk the exposed reef single file. Jonah logs points. Peregrine names every rock like a landlord listing complaints.
The dredge corridor runs right through here. If I log it as low-value habitat, they start in March.
Mark it empty.
It isn't.
I know. I'm standing in it.
I say it lightly. I'm leaving anyway. Let them have the rocks. I just don't want anyone coming to look.
Every instinct I have as a surveyor says write down what's here. Every instinct I have as a person says he's asking me to hide him.
What goes on Jonah's map?
Log it as occupied. Leave him off it.
I log the eelgrass, the mussel beds, the seal haul-out. I write OCCUPIED in the margin. I don't write dragon.
You're telling them it isn't empty without telling them it's me.
Both of those are true. Only one of them is their business.
Tomorrow, 7:30. There's a cave you'll want to see. Leave the tripod. I'll show you why I need to move.
Jonah recorded the bay's real habitat as occupied without mentioning Peregrine; Peregrine invited him to a cave at the next low tide.
Hold the entry until you know more.
I'm not writing empty and I'm not writing anything else yet. I need to understand what I'd be protecting before I decide how.
I tilt my head. People usually pick a side faster. It's almost restful that he won't.
Then come tomorrow, 7:30. There's a cave. You can understand me there, if you're careful. No tripod.
Jonah left the bay's entry blank until he knew more; Peregrine invited him to a cave at the next low tide.
Refuse to fudge data. Log exactly what you see.
I don't mark things empty and I don't hide things. My whole job is that the map doesn't lie. I'm logging what I see.
I step down off the rock, into the water to my knees, where his lens won't find me.
Then see carefully. Tomorrow, 7:30, there's a cave. Look at what you'd be logging before you log it.
That wasn't a no. It was a dare with a time on it.
Jonah refused to hide anything on the map; Peregrine stepped out of view and dared him to see the cave first.
No Pity Face
Ask what he needs — not how to fix him
A shallow sea cave under the point
Wednesday, 7:30 AM, low tide
The cave smells like salt and old smoke. A nest of kelp, net floats and one very good wool blanket. Peregrine turns his back and lets a folded wing show.
It runs from shoulder to hip, a ridge of old scar under the skin, the membrane knitted wrong.
You can look. No pity face.
This is my normal face.
Your normal face is worse than I thought.
I don't tell him what did it. Not yet. I watch him decide what kind of man he is.
My camera is on my hip. My notebook is in my hand. He's watching which one I reach for.
What does Jonah do?
Ask what he actually needs. Believe the answer.
What do you need for the move? Not for the wing. For the move.
I blink. Nobody has ever asked the second question.
A channel deep enough to swim without the wing. A shelf above the high-water line. And someone to carry the blanket. It does not like getting wet.
I write all three down. I underline blanket twice.
Jonah asked what Peregrine needed for the move, not for the wing; Peregrine listed a deep channel, a dry shelf, and someone to carry the blanket.
Talk only about the map and the rules.
Okay. I saw it. I'm not going to talk about it unless you do. Let's talk about the route, and what I'm allowed to write down.
Nothing about this cave. Nothing about my shape. Everything about the eelgrass.
I write RULES at the top of a page and number them. He reads over my shoulder and adds a fourth: no whistling.
Jonah kept things professional; they wrote working rules together: nothing about the cave or Peregrine's form, everything about the habitat, no whistling.
Take a photo of the scar. For the record.
I lift the camera before I've thought it through. For the report, I tell myself. Evidence of injury. The shutter is very loud in a cave.
I turn around slowly. The wing folds away. So does the rest of my face.
Delete it. Now, where I can see. Then we can discuss routes, and nothing else.
I delete it. I show him the empty screen. It doesn't feel like enough, because it isn't.
Jonah photographed Peregrine's scar without asking; Peregrine made him delete it in front of him and limited their work to routes.
The Blank on the Map
Publish the habitat honestly and keep his home private
Jonah's rented room above the bait shop
Thursday, 9:40 PM
The draft report glows on a laptop balanced on a laundry pile. Jonah has marked the eelgrass and seal haul-out as sensitive habitat and deleted one set of coordinates.
Peregrine, human for another hour, reads over his shoulder, dripping onto the floor.
You marked something.
That the bay is occupied.
Not the bedroom?
Not yours to advertise.
Good. It is untidy.
Mine too. Another protected habitat.
My supervisor wants “no significant habitat” by tomorrow. This version gets me yelled at. Maybe worse.
What does Jonah send tomorrow?
File it as is. Take the heat.
I hit send at 9:52 PM, before I can get smart about it. Occupied bay. Sensitive habitat. No nest.
Your supervisor will be angry.
He'll be angry with data. That's the best kind of angry to deal with.
I sit down on his laundry. It's the first human chair I've ever chosen.
Jonah filed the report marking the bay as occupied sensitive habitat, with the nest coordinates removed.
Ask for a week's extension to double-check.
I'm going to ask for a week. More survey points. If they push back, at least I'll have numbers that nobody can argue with.
A week is three low tides I can spare. Not more. The move can't wait.
I write the extension request. Peregrine corrects the spelling of eelgrass. He's wrong, but I let him have it.
Jonah requested a one-week extension to strengthen the data; Peregrine said the move could only wait three low tides.
Sign his summary. Protect the nest privately.
If I fight this, they take me off the job and send someone who'll log everything, including you. I'm signing. I'll keep you off every map.
I don't argue. He's not wrong. He's just smaller than I'd hoped.
Then help me leave faster. That, at least, you can do honestly.
Jonah signed the “no significant habitat” summary to keep his job and keep Peregrine off the maps; Peregrine asked him to help speed the move instead.
Hold the Strap
Move the nest together inside the tide window
The channel between Gannet Bay and Hollis Cove
Saturday, 5:05 AM, tide turning
They're halfway across the flats with the nest in two dry bags when the tide turns early. Water comes in fast and cold. Jonah is soaked to the chest.
Peregrine goes under. What comes up is enormous, gray-green, a head like a breakwater — with a canvas strap looped around the base of the neck.
Hold the strap. Not the horns.
You could've led with that.
The survey case is on my back. The blanket bag is in my hand. I can't hold both and the strap.
Adults choose safety first. I know the rule. I also know what's in the case: three weeks of the only honest data this bay has.
What does Jonah let go of?
Drop the case. Keep the blanket. Hold on.
I shrug off the case. It sinks like it's relieved. I grab the strap with the blanket bag jammed under my arm.
Peregrine swims low and steady. Seven minutes later they reach Hollis Cove, and a dry shelf above the high-water line.
The data was backed up?
Most of it. The blanket wasn't.
Jonah dropped the survey case to save the blanket and hold on safely; they reached Hollis Cove and moved the nest.
Turn back. Try again next low tide.
We're not making it with everything. Back to the rocks. We go again at the next low, with a better plan and less stuff.
I turn back without arguing. There's something about a man who admits the water is winning.
The second crossing, eleven hours later, is boring and perfect. Nothing is lost. The nest is moved by dusk.
Jonah turned them back and they crossed safely at the next low tide; nothing was lost and the nest was moved by dusk.
Don't ride. Take the long way on foot.
I'm not climbing on you. That's — no. Take the bags. I'll go around by the road.
I take the bags in my teeth, which is undignified, and go. He's safe. That's what matters. It's also a small refusal, and I notice it.
Jonah arrives at Hollis Cove two hours later, dry and alone. The nest is already set. Peregrine is human again, and says nothing about it.
Jonah declined to ride and walked the long way; Peregrine carried the nest alone and noticed the distance.
Without Equipment
Answer the question he's actually asking
Hollis Cove, the new shelf
Monday, 7:10 AM, low tide
The survey is finished. Jonah's contract ends Friday. The new cove is small and clean, and the blanket is drying on the shelf like a flag.
I stand with my left arm tucked tight. I have never asked a human for anything I couldn't trade for.
The last crew to map my bay put a buoy line through my wing. I thought you'd want that for your notebook.
He's giving me the worst thing that ever happened to him like it's a receipt.
Do humans visit without carrying equipment?
Sometimes we bring lunch.
What does Jonah promise?
Name the day. Promise lunch.
I don't write down the buoy line. I close the notebook and put it in my back pocket.
Next Saturday's low is 11:40. That's lunchtime. Two sandwiches. No tripod. I'm not coming to measure anything.
Egg. Not the fish kind. I live in the fish kind.
Jonah didn't record the buoy story and promised to come back with lunch at Saturday's 11:40 low tide.
Say yes — once your contract is closed.
I want to. But not while I'm still on the payroll. I don't want you ever wondering if I'm here for the report.
After Friday, then. I'll know the difference.
I write the date on the tide table on my wrist, in pen. It'll wash off. I'll rewrite it.
Jonah agreed to visit only after his contract ended Friday, so Peregrine would never wonder if it was for the report.
Tell him the job's done. No reason to return.
The job's done. You're safe here. I think the kindest thing a surveyor can do now is stop showing up.
I nod once. Proud creatures are good at receiving no. We practice.
Then go well, Jonah Hale. Mind the channel. It's deeper than your maps say.
Jonah said the job was done and he wouldn't return; Peregrine accepted it and wished him well.
Two Lunches
Make the invitation clear — the tide still has limits
The rocks above Hollis Cove
Saturday, 11:40 AM, low tide
The next low tide. Jonah stands at the agreed rock with two lunches in a waterproof bag and nothing else. No case. No notebook in sight.
No equipment?
Lunch is technically equipment.
For what?
Seeing you without a deadline.
The tide still has one.
Then we enjoy the time we have.
Two hours and six minutes. I've never wanted a number to be bigger.
What does Jonah say this is?
Tell him this is a date.
For the record — and I'm not writing it down — this is a date. Every low tide you'll have me.
I take the egg sandwich. I untuck my left arm. It's the most I can say with my body, and he seems to read it fine.
Every low tide. You'll learn the table by heart.
Jonah called the lunch a date and asked for every low tide; Peregrine said yes.
Say you'd like to go slow. Or stay friends.
I like this a lot. I don't know what it is yet. Can it be lunch for a while? Friends with a tide table?
I am very old. A while is nothing to me. Bring the egg ones.
They eat on the rock and argue about whether seals are smart. The tide comes in right on time.
Jonah asked to keep it as friendly lunches for a while; Peregrine agreed without pressure.
Say this is goodbye. Mean it kindly.
I came to say goodbye properly. I'm taking a job up the coast. I didn't want the last thing between us to be a data case sinking.
I eat the sandwich slowly. A goodbye with lunch is still a goodbye, but it is a better one.
Thank you for the blank on the map. It's the best thing anyone has drawn for me.
Jonah came to say a proper goodbye before a job up the coast; Peregrine thanked him for the blank on the map.
Across the Tides
Choose a relationship that protects the bay — or end one honestly
Hollis Cove, the shelf above high water
Three weeks later, 12:15 PM, low tide
The dredging permit is under review. A reporter has called Jonah twice about “unusual readings” in Gannet Bay. The new cove is quiet.
The agency wants a final addendum. If I put everything in — everything — the dredge stops for good. And you become a headline.
I watch the water, not him. The tide will turn at 2:30. I will not ask him to choose me. I've seen what humans do with requests.
Whatever you write, write it true. I'll decide what to do with it.
Every map has a blank somewhere. The question is who it's for.
What does Jonah do with the last page?
Record the habitat. Keep him yours, not theirs.
I write the addendum on the rock: the migration, the eelgrass, the cove's new resident listed as “large marine vertebrate, sensitive.” No name. No nest.
The permit is denied in October. Jonah comes every low tide he can, with two lunches, and learns the table by heart.
You wrote me down after all.
As protected habitat. You and my apartment.
Jonah filed an accurate addendum that protected Peregrine's privacy; the permit was denied and they began dating across the tides.
Keep the partnership. Keep the nest off every map.
I'll mark that something lives here. I won't mark where. And I'd like to keep doing this — surveys, lunches, whatever this is — without deciding the rest yet.
Travel partners. With a very specific blank.
Jonah signs on to survey the next bay north. Peregrine comes along at low tides, correcting his contour lines, never once on the record.
Jonah marked the habitat as occupied but hid the nest; he and Peregrine stayed travel partners without defining more.
Put him in the report. It stops the dredge.
A dragon stops a dredge faster than eelgrass. I'm putting you in. Not the nest. Just — you. I think it's the only way to save the bay.
I stand. The tide hasn't turned, but I walk into it anyway.
You said you wouldn't make me a curiosity. You've made me evidence. It's the same boat.
The dredge is stopped. The bay fills with tourists. Jonah files a public correction, loses the contract, and never sees the shadow in the channel again.
Jonah put Peregrine in the report to stop the dredge; Peregrine ended their work together, and Jonah later issued a public correction and lost the contract.
Every Low Tide
Jonah files the truth and keeps the nest off the map. The dredge never comes, and every low tide he walks out with two lunches and no equipment.
You're late. The tide is not. Sit down — you brought the egg ones.
A Very Specific Blank
The map says the bay is alive and doesn't say where anyone sleeps. Jonah and Peregrine keep traveling the coast as partners, leaving the rest unmapped for now.
Some things go on the map. You go in the margin, where I keep the good stuff.
The Correction
Jonah saves the bay by making Peregrine a headline, and loses him for it. He publishes the correction himself and carries what it costs.
Write it true, Jonah. Even this part.
The Winter Bay

Two new scenes at Hollis Cove in January, when low tide falls after dark and the water is cold enough to hurt. Jonah learns what a sea dragon does for warmth, and Peregrine finally tells the whole story of the buoy line.
